title: Why spacecraft go to die at Point Nemo
sentences: There is a spot in the Pacific Ocean so remote, the nearest humans are often in space.
It is called Point Nemo, about 2,700 kilometres from the closest land.
When the International Space Station passes overhead, its crew is closer than anyone on Earth.
That loneliness makes it perfect for one job: a graveyard for spacecraft.
Since 1971, hundreds of old satellites and cargo ships have been steered down here.
The Russian space station Mir broke apart and sank in this region in 2001.
One day, the International Space Station itself is planned to fall here too.
Would you sail out to the loneliest place on the planet?

title: Why humans can't dig deeper than 12 kilometres
sentences: The deepest hole humans ever dug is narrower than a dinner plate.
It is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, about 12.2 kilometres deep.
Scientists expected cool rock, but at the bottom it reached around 180 degrees Celsius.
At that heat and pressure, rock behaved almost like thick plastic and kept closing the hole.
They also found water locked inside the crystals, far deeper than anyone predicted.
After nearly twenty years of drilling, the project stopped in 1992.
Even this record only scratched about a third of the way through the crust.
How deep do you think we will ever really go?

title: Why space is freezing if the Sun is so hot
sentences: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, yet space is brutally cold.
The secret is that heat needs something to travel through.
On Earth, air and water carry heat from atom to atom.
Space is almost a perfect vacuum, with nearly nothing to carry it.
So sunlight only heats what it hits directly.
That's why the sunny side of the space station can pass 120 degrees, while the shade drops far below freezing.
Astronauts survive with suits that reflect light and carefully move heat around.
Hot and freezing at the same time. Which side would you pick?

title: Where your files really go when you press delete
sentences: When you delete a file, it usually isn't gone.
Your computer mostly erases the label that says where the file lives.
The actual data stays on the drive, marked as space that can be reused.
Until something new is written on top, recovery tools can often bring it back.
That's how investigators rescue photos from old memory cards.
Modern solid state drives can clean up deleted blocks on their own, so recovery is harder there.
To truly wipe a device, use its full reset or encryption before you sell it.
Did you know your old phone might still remember?

title: How the internet crosses the ocean floor
sentences: Your messages to another continent most likely don't go through space.
They travel through cables lying on the ocean floor.
Undersea cables carry the vast majority of international internet traffic.
Inside, hair thin glass fibres carry pulses of light across thousands of kilometres.
Near the shore, cables are wrapped in steel and buried to resist anchors and fishing nets.
In the deep sea, they can be about as thick as a garden hose.
Repair ships with grappling hooks fix breaks, sometimes in water kilometres deep.
Next time a video loads, remember it may have crossed an ocean floor.

title: What really happens to a human body in space without a suit
sentences: In movies, people in space explode. That is not what happens.
Your skin is strong enough to hold your body together.
But with no air pressure, the moisture on your tongue and eyes would begin to boil.
The air in your lungs would rush out, so you should never hold your breath.
Your body would swell, but not burst.
Within about fifteen seconds, you would lose consciousness from lack of oxygen.
In a 1966 NASA test accident, a man exposed to near vacuum survived because pressure returned fast.
Knowing this, would you still take a spacewalk?

title: Why drinking seawater makes you thirstier
sentences: You could be surrounded by ocean and still die of thirst.
Seawater is roughly three and a half percent salt.
That is much saltier than your blood.
Your kidneys can only make urine that's less salty than seawater.
So to flush out the salt from one cup, your body has to spend more water than you drank.
Every sip makes you more dehydrated, not less.
That's why sailors carried fresh water, and lifeboats now carry desalination kits.
Would you trust a survival plan that relied on rain?

title: Why you jerk awake just as you fall asleep
sentences: You're drifting off, then suddenly your body jolts like you fell off a cliff.
That is called a hypnic jerk, and most people have felt it.
As you fall asleep, your muscles relax and your brain begins switching off.
Sometimes the brain misreads that sudden relaxation as falling.
It fires a quick burst to the muscles, and you wake with a start.
Caffeine, stress and tiredness can make it happen more often.
One popular idea says it's an old reflex from ancestors sleeping in trees, but that's still unproven.
When was the last time it happened to you?

title: What happens if you fall into Jupiter?
sentences: Jupiter has no solid surface to land on.
Falling in, you'd first drop through ammonia clouds at hundreds of kilometres per hour.
Winds there can blow faster than any hurricane on Earth.
As you sink, the pressure rises and the air thickens into a hot, crushing soup.
Deeper still, hydrogen is squeezed until it behaves like a liquid metal.
No probe has ever survived the trip. Galileo's probe lasted under an hour.
Jupiter is less a planet you stand on, and more a giant you dissolve into.
Would you rather fall into Jupiter or a black hole?

title: Why fast charging slows down after 80 percent
sentences: Your phone races to 80 percent, then crawls to 100. That's on purpose.
Charging pushes lithium ions into the battery, like filling seats in a stadium.
When most seats are empty, ions can rush in fast.
As it fills up, the last ions have to squeeze into the few seats left.
Forcing them in fast would heat the battery and wear it out.
So the charger slows down to protect it.
Many phones now offer settings that stop around 80 percent to extend battery life.
Do you charge to 100 every night?

title: The lake hidden under 4 kilometres of Antarctic ice
sentences: Under the Antarctic ice lies a lake bigger than many countries' largest lakes.
It's called Lake Vostok, buried under about four kilometres of ice.
It has been sealed off from sunlight and air for possibly millions of years.
Heat from the Earth below and the weight of the ice keep it liquid.
In 2012, Russian scientists finally drilled down to touch its surface.
Researchers are looking for microbes that may have lived there in total isolation.
Places like this help scientists imagine life under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa.
Should we open sealed places like this, or leave them untouched?

title: Why you never actually touch anything
sentences: Right now you think you're touching your phone. In a way, you're not.
Everything is made of atoms, wrapped in clouds of electrons.
Electrons carry negative charge, and like charges push each other away.
When your finger meets the screen, those electron clouds repel.
What you feel as touch is that electric push, not atoms crashing together.
Physicists add that 'touch' only means atoms getting close enough to interact.
So you're always resting a tiny distance above the chair you sit on.
Does that make you feel any different about touching things?

title: Where old airplanes go when they retire
sentences: When airlines retire a plane, many end up in the desert.
Places like the Mojave in California hold hundreds of parked jets.
Dry air means less rust, so the planes stay in good condition for years.
Some are stored to fly again when demand returns.
Others are stripped for engines, seats and parts worth millions.
The rest are cut up, and the aluminium is recycled.
Next to Tucson, the US military's boneyard holds thousands of aircraft.
Would you visit a desert full of sleeping jets?

title: Why time runs faster on a mountain
sentences: Your head is aging slightly faster than your feet.
Einstein predicted that gravity slows down time.
The closer you are to Earth's mass, the slower your clock ticks.
Atomic clocks have measured this difference over a height of just one foot.
On a mountain top, you would age a few billionths of a second faster each day.
GPS satellites have to correct for this, or maps would drift by kilometres every day.
Time isn't the same everywhere. It depends on where you stand.
Would you live on a mountain to age faster, or the beach to age slower?
